title: Private trackers
description: One section per private tracker: the rules that bind it, and the numbers those rules make matter.

panels.title: Accounts below their own line
panels.description: Every tracker measured against its own threshold: TorrentLeech disables under 0.4, DigitalCore revokes leeching under 0.5, C411 blocks downloads under 0.8. Anything above zero means an account is on the wrong side of a wall.

targets.expr: count(((tracker_ratio or tracker_read_ratio) / tracker_min_ratio) < 1) or vector(0)

panels.title: Tightest headroom, and where
panels.description: The smallest amount of non-freeleech downloading left on any account, and which one it is. This is the number that decides what may be grabbed by hand.

panels.title: Obligations with the clock stopped
panels.description: Every tracker. A torrent that owes seeding time and is not announcing pays nothing off, and on DigitalCore one hour of silence is enough to be listed.

panels.title: TorrentLeech ratio
panels.description:
Named because it is the only account under a deadline. Its line is 0.4.

Between 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-24 these numbers came from the parked `trackers/stats.py`, pushed under the job `tracker_stats`; since then they come from the tracker-control service. Two producers means two series per tracker, which drew two of everything. `max by (tracker)` stitches them into one line, so the history before the switch is kept rather than filtered out.

panels.title: Grabs a day, all grabbers
panels.description: Across every enabled autobrr filter, read from autobrr itself rather than assumed. Each grab is locked on disk until its hit & run window closes, so this is a disk budget as much as a rate.

panels.title: Last tracker-control run
panels.description: How long ago tracker-control last read the sites and moved its levers. It runs every 30 minutes, so anything much past that means the service is stuck, and a stale reading looks exactly like a healthy account. This is the age of the scraped figures; the hand-read ones have their own panel below.

panels.title: What each site asks, and what is configured against it

options.content:
| Tracker | The site asks | Configured | Margin | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| TorrentLeech | 240 h or ratio 1.0 | 15 d, ratio 1.2 | 120 h | The widest clock gap measured here, 26 to 118 h |
| DigitalCore | 120 h, clock starts at 10% | 180 h, ratio 1.0 | 60 h | Their gap read off My Seeds: 9 to 23 h |
| C411 | 72 h plus 24 h of grace | 150 h, ratio 1.0 | 54 h | H&R disabled site-wide, so a thinner margin is affordable |
| retrotoon | 72 h, **no ratio rule at all** | 120 h, no ratio limit | 48 h | Only time clears anything here |
| anything stalled | — | gone 12 h after the last byte | — | It never seeded, so no group would ever release it |

Every margin exists because qBittorrent counts seeding time while announces are rejected and the site does not. Full rules per site in [docs/private-trackers.md](https://github.com/PlatanosVerdes/rpi-homeserver/blob/main/docs/private-trackers.md), the lifecycle in [docs/lifecycle.md](https://github.com/PlatanosVerdes/rpi-homeserver/blob/main/docs/lifecycle.md).

panels.title: Ratio, per account
panels.description: The same figure each account's own section shows, so it cannot be misread as anything else. What differs per site is the colour, because each has a different wall: TorrentLeech disables under 0.4, DigitalCore revokes leeching under 0.5, C411 blocks downloads under 0.8. Red is below the line, orange is just above it, green is clear of it. The bar tops out at 1.5 so the accounts near their wall stay readable; the number beside it is always the true value. Sites with no ratio rule are absent by design.

panels.title: Headroom
panels.description: How many GB of non-freeleech downloading still fits before the account crosses the line the site disables it under: (uploaded - min_ratio x downloaded) / min_ratio. This is where each account stands right now; the same figure over time is in the History row.

panels.title: Open hit and run obligations
panels.description: Measured from the client against each site's own rule, not read from the sites: the only H&R number any of them publishes here is DigitalCore's, and that one is read by eye. Normal for anything recent. Only the stopped-clock count is an emergency.

panels.title: Clock stopped
panels.description: Owing hours while not announcing. The only one of these that is an emergency: flat at zero is the only acceptable shape.

panels.title: Age of each hand-read figure
panels.description:
How old the by-eye reading is, for the accounts that still need one. A site whose login works drops off this panel, because its entry in readings.json becomes a fallback that is meant to go stale, and one whose login breaks reappears here.

retrotoon will always be here: its login sits behind Cloudflare Turnstile. C411 is here while its password is wrong. TorrentLeech and DigitalCore read themselves, and the age of those figures is "Last tracker-control run".

panels.title: What each account has given, and earned
Seeding on disk
panels.description: What this tracker's torrents occupy locally right now, per the client. The trend is in the History row.

panels.title: Torrents seeding
panels.description: How many torrents are seeding for this account right now, per the client.

panels.title: Uploaded, per the client
panels.description: What the client says it has sent for this account, which is not what the site credits: multipliers and freeleech make the two diverge. The trend is in the History row.

panels.title: Uploaded, per the site
panels.description:
What the site credits, which is not what the client sent: upload multipliers and freeleech make the two diverge, and only this one moves the ratio.

Between 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-24 these numbers came from the parked `trackers/stats.py`, pushed under the job `tracker_stats`; since then they come from the tracker-control service. Two producers means two series per tracker, which drew two of everything. `max by (tracker)` stitches them into one line, so the history before the switch is kept rather than filtered out.

panels.title: Bonus points
panels.description: What the bonus shop has to spend. Read by eye, so trust it as much as the reading age above.

panels.title: Leech bonus
panels.description: DigitalCore only: the percentage off what every download costs against ratio, earned by seeding. 100% is a site-wide freeleech.

panels.title: Hours each torrent still owes
panels.description: Per torrent, per tracker, and whether its clock is running. A stopped clock on a torrent that still owes hours is the only row worth reacting to.

panels.title: Grabs a day, per tracker
panels.description: Zero means the filter exists and is switched off, which is different from having no grabber at all.

panels.title: TorrentLeech ratio against its line
panels.description:
TorrentLeech only, because it is the one account with a deadline and the only one whose ratio can be scraped. Both series are filtered to it: without that, `tracker_min_ratio` returned every site's threshold and drew three different lines all labelled "the line".

Between 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-24 these numbers came from the parked `trackers/stats.py`, pushed under the job `tracker_stats`; since then they come from the tracker-control service. Two producers means two series per tracker, which drew two of everything. `max by (tracker)` stitches them into one line, so the history before the switch is kept rather than filtered out.

panels.title: Headroom, over time
panels.description:
The same headroom as the row above, over time. A line walking down is an account spending faster than it earns, which is the shape worth catching early.

Between 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-24 these numbers came from the parked `trackers/stats.py`, pushed under the job `tracker_stats`; since then they come from the tracker-control service. Two producers means two series per tracker, which drew two of everything. `max by (tracker)` stitches them into one line, so the history before the switch is kept rather than filtered out.

panels.title: Seeding on disk, over time
panels.description:
Bytes held per tracker over time. A step down is a retention group letting something go; a slope up is the grabber outrunning the deletions.

Between 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-24 these numbers came from the parked `trackers/stats.py`, pushed under the job `tracker_stats`; since then they come from the tracker-control service. Two producers means two series per tracker, which drew two of everything. `max by (tracker)` stitches them into one line, so the history before the switch is kept rather than filtered out.

A tracker that no longer exists keeps a line that simply ends: btschool was removed on 2026-08-24, so it is history rather than a ghost.

panels.title: Uploaded per the client, over time
panels.description:
What the client has sent per account over time. Flat means nothing is being asked of these torrents, which is normal on a private tracker with no leechers.

panels.description:
Torrents that have not yet cleared their tracker's seed requirement, measured from qBittorrent against each site's rule. The client's clock runs ahead of the tracker's, by 26 to 118 h the last time the two were compared, so read this as a floor. Only the panel beside it is an emergency.

panels.description:
DigitalCore's own formula applied to what is seeding. Cross-seeds move this at no disk cost.

panels.title: How much leaves the house each month
Uploaded a month, at this week's rate
panels.description: Bytes leaving the qBittorrent container over the last seven days, scaled to thirty. cAdvisor counts the container's own interface, so this is wire bytes: torrent payload plus protocol overhead, plus the WebUI and *arr API traffic sharing that interface. The counter is per container instance, so `sum` is what survives a recreate. The window is a week and not a month because Prometheus here keeps 15 days.

panels.title: Share of a 10 TB egress allowance
panels.description: The same monthly figure against 10 TB, the outbound transfer an Oracle Always Free tenancy includes per month. It answers whether the seed path would fit if it were tunnelled through that instance. It says nothing about the home line, whose upload is unchanged either way, because the bytes still leave the house first.

panels.title: Share of it the sites credit
panels.description: What the private trackers credited over the same week as a share of everything the client sent. The remainder is upload no configured account is claiming, which is public-tracker traffic. Credited bytes carry upload multipliers, so this can read high without more bytes on the wire. `max by (tracker)` collapses the two producers each tracker has.

panels.title: Uploaded per day
panels.description: A rolling 24-hour total of the same wire bytes, so a spike is a day that seeded hard rather than a scrape landing badly.
